title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
** Maine is one of the least populated states and is the most forested in the entire country, which means people are spread apart with long distances to travel. In this analysis, I look at the travel time to work across counties in Maine, and test the reliability of the data between each area.**

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Most margins of error are in the 1.5-4.75% range relative to the estimate.
Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

# observe spread of MOE percentage valuess
hist(county_data$moe_pct)









county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2.5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 3.5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"

# A tibble: 3 × 2

  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     4
2 Low confidence      4
3 Moderate            8


For these counties, the margin of error percentage was relatively low, which meant using the 5% and 10% cutoffs for high and moderate confidence were unsuitable. Instead, a 2.5% cutoff was used for high confidence and 3.5% was used for moderate confidence instead. 4 counties had high and low confidence, while 8 had moderate confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 23001 Androscoggin County, Maine  48226   1013 112323    NA
2 23003 Aroostook County, Maine     26005    704  67227    NA
3 23005 Cumberland County, Maine   134152   2045 305940    NA
4 23007 Franklin County, Maine      12103    543  30145    NA
5 23009 Hancock County, Maine       23866    701  56084    NA
6 23011 Kennebec County, Maine      51512   1295 125614    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2.5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 3.5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          4        196641.
2 Low confidence           4         30051.
3 Moderate                 8         58829 


The average population for high confidence counties were many times higher than other confidence categories. Counties with low confidence had the lowest average population by far. Based on these results, higher populations may produce more representative data, as outliers are better dealt with in larger sample sizes.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy



Maine Counties and Cities Map


The following counties had the highest margin of error (in order): Piscataquis, Franklin, Sagadahoc, and Lincoln county. These counties had some of the lowest populations in the entire state. Generally, smaller sample sizes yield more frequent outliers and a normal distribution is less expected due to the lack of “average” samples. Counties with the highest confidence were the most populous. These counties included Cumberland, Androscoggin, Penobscot, and York. York and Cumberland are the most southern counties, which make them that much closer to the rest of New England. Cumberland is also home to the better Portland and Bowdoin College. Interestingly, counties that had colleges outside of Portland, such as Bates, UMaine, or Colby, had higher confidences. With the presence of these colleges, population counting is more accurate. Ignoring margins of error can be harmful, especially when the data may not be representative of the target population. In this case, the time spent traveling in a low reliability county may not actually be accurate. Hypothetically, if this county actually had a much higher travel time to work compared to what the data says, they may not get the appropriate allocation of funding for infrastructure and road development. This can be harmful when the data says another county has high travel time, despite that not being true, which can lead to funding cuts for a county that actually needs it.

title: Week 3: ggplot & errors
text:
Key Concepts

Coefficient of variation (CV)

Relative measure of sampling error
Low CV < 15% –> high reliability
Medium CV = 15-30% –> moderate reliability
High CV > 30% –> low reliability



Measures of Uncertainty

Standard error (SE): MOE / 1.645
Derived uncertainty: margins of error of numerator and denominator can’t be simply computed

moe_sum -> adding estimates together
moe_prop -> one estimate as share of another
moe_ratio -> one not a subset of another




Change Over Time

Compare non-overlapping intervals: calculate change between intervals and uncertainty of both estimates
SE_diff: sqrt(SE1^2 + SE2^2)
CI of Change: Difference +- (1.645 * SE_diff)
CV = (SE / Estimate) x 100
z = change / SE_diff
significant = abs(z) > 1.645

The article claims a 14% increase in poverty rate between the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 ACS data in the neighborhood of Eastwick, a 17% increase in poverty rate in Holmesburg, a drop in median household income in Tioga-Nicetown, and a 61% poverty rate in Fairhill.
The article pointed variables of interest from the census tract: total poverty rate, white poverty rate, median household income, and white population. Data from the 5-year ACS (2006-2010 & 2013-2017) and 2016 1-year ACS were used. The article states using these data tables while referencing the 2016-2017 ACS as the then-newest census data. I assumed some of the time period for some of the claims: Fairhill, Holmesburg, Tioga-Nicetown and the income gap. No years were specified for these so I assumed 2013-2017 based on the title. The time periods that overlap are 2013-2017 and 2016-2017. However, the 1-year ACS data is not available at the tract level due to the area 65,000 population requirement. This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

First, I would have liked to look at bus ridership since it has more overall coverage, but there were no data for 2023. The feature that lowered CV RMSE the most was distance to the Northeast Philadelphia Airport. This was reflected in the residuals around the airport decreasing in the second residual plot. The abundance of public transit in the forms of regional rail and L1 likely made this area a strong outlier in terms of public transit commuters. In comparison, other jobs around the city likely has less accessible public transit, making workers consider different options. The travel time category was the most disappointing because there was a weak positive relationship with the variable of interest observed in the correlation coefficient and scatter plot. Conceptually, this relationship makes sense, since longer travel times mean gas may not be efficient, so taking public transport would be the better option. However, adding the travel time categories actually made the prediction slightly worse. This could be due to the cutoff at each level not being representative and the variable is better as a continuous predictor.
For every mile closer to a college, the % of people taking public transport to work decreases by 1.27%. When comparing tracts A and B, if A was 1 mile away from a college, the model predicts tract A to have 1.27% less people taking public transport.
There are 3 census tracts that had extreme residuals that I would like to look at: one in West Philly, tracts in Brewery town, and one near NE airport. The tracts in West Philly and NE airport were over predicted, so I would want to look more closely at traffic congestion and road infrastructure since these variables are closely tied to whether or not a person decides to use a car. Using Google Street Map view could be a way to personally verify this, but the city of Philadelphia likely has data on these variables. For the tracts in Brewery town, getting the number of businesses and looking at the zoning ordinance to approximate how many go there for work would be the next step to prevent under predicting. The zoning ordinance and businesses geodata should be available on the opendataphilly website.
Since the CV of most data points are very low, it is unlikely due to statistical noise, but rather model error. For example, the samples that were a big miss also had relatively low CVs. The line does not indicate there is a trend in the estimate CV and the residual size. In conclusion, model training has to be more comprehensive to reduce the errors.

title: Week 4: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
Key concepts

Joining

join function: joins two tables by a column for rows that match
left/right_join: keep all observations in x/y
inner_join: only keep observations that are in both
full_join: keep observations in both
anti_join: keep observations that don’t match between two tables



Geometry

shp: shape file
gdb: geodatabase
sf: simple features



Coordinate reference systems (CRS)
The Earth is a geoid, which is an imperfect circle, that can be approximated with an ellipsoid (projection). Different flattening ratios for each CRS.

NAD27: Clarke’s ellipsoid marked at Meades Ranch, KS (degrees)
NAD83: GRS-80 reference system, Earth-centered (degrees)
WGS84: Earth-centered (GPS standard)
Albers equal area (meters)



Ways to project

cylindrical: based on latitude with no distortion
transverse cylindrical: based on longitude with straight line of tangency
conic: curved line of tangency
planar: circular line of tangency
conformal conic: good for high latitude countries



what to preserve and what projection to use

Shapes: conformal conic (especially good for high latitude countries)
Areas: equal-area
Distance: equal-distance
Direction: :(

Geographic - units:degrees
Projected - good for local mapping - units: feet` or meters


R

st_set_crs(): relabel
st_transform(): change CRS
st_crs(): get CRS
st_buffer(): inner buffer of geometry
st_intersects(): do two geometry objects intersect
st_touches(): one point in common but not intersecting
st_within(): does every of A lie in B
st_filter(): subset by spatial feature
st_intersection(): returns intersection of two geometries
st_union(): merge two geometries with no overlap
st_join(): combine two objects based on geometric relationship
st_distance(): return minimum distance between two objects

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_intersects)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 238


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?
It’s more likely a model failure because the size of the residual has nothing to do with the reliability of data. There were very reliable estimates with much higher residuals.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(6950)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_higherEd + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
234.8236 331.9546 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $___ per month.”
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.
The training RMSE should be lower because the model was trained on that data. RMSE is expected to be higher on new data.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_higherEd + n_stations,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

Part 7: Where is the model wrong?

7A: Residuals vs. fitted

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = fitted_m2, y = resid_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted rent", y = "Residual (actual − predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()







bptest(m2)


    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  m2
BP = 13.683, df = 4, p-value = 0.00838


Stop and look: Random cloud, funnel, or curve? If it’s a funnel, the predictions aren’t biased, but one RMSE hides the fact that the model misses by much more in some tracts. Which tracts?
Visually there is no pattern, but the BP test was significant, which means we reject the null hypothesis (homoscedasticity).


7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m2), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")








Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.
A lot of red in center city, south philly, northwest philly, and northeast philly. A lot of blue in west philly.

text:
Part 7: Reflection

First, I would have liked to look at bus ridership since it has more overall coverage, but there were no data for 2023. The feature that lowered CV RMSE the most was distance to the Northeast Philadelphia Airport. This was reflected in the residuals around the airport decreasing in the second residual plot. The abundance of public transit in the forms of regional rail and L1 likely made this area a strong outlier in terms of public transit commuters. In comparison, other jobs around the city likely has less accessible public transit, making workers consider different options. The travel time category was the most disappointing because there was a weak positive relationship with the variable of interest observed in the correlation coefficient and scatter plot. Conceptually, this relationship makes sense, since longer travel times mean gas may not be efficient, so taking public transport would be the better option. However, adding the travel time categories actually made the prediction slightly worse. This could be due to the cutoff at each level not being representative and the variable is better as a continuous predictor. I was also disappointed by the proximity to a regional rail, as that should had have a big effect on workers travelling long distances.
For every mile closer to a college, the % of people taking public transport to work decreases by 1.27%. When comparing tracts A and B, if A was 1 mile away from a college, the model predicts tract A to have 1.27% less people taking public transport.
There are 3 census tracts that had extreme residuals that I would like to look at: one in West Philly, tracts in Brewery town, and one near NE airport. The tracts in West Philly and NE airport were over predicted, so I would want to look more closely at traffic congestion and road infrastructure since these variables are closely tied to whether or not a person decides to use a car. Using Google Street Map view could be a way to personally verify this, but the city of Philadelphia likely has data on these variables. For the tracts in Brewery town, getting the number of businesses and looking at the zoning ordinance to approximate how many go there for work would be the next step to prevent under predicting. The zoning ordinance and businesses geodata should be available on the opendataphilly website.
Since the CV of most data points are very low, it is unlikely due to statistical noise, but rather model error. For example, the samples that were a big miss also had relatively low CVs. The line does not indicate there is a trend in the estimate CV and the residual size. In conclusion, model training has to be more comprehensive to reduce the errors.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

Your answer:
First, the dependent variable is extremely skewed. There are very few houses that sell for many times the price of a median house and very few that are sold at extremely low prices. Because these houses likely don’t represent the standard single-family housing, these outliers should be removed for prediction. Furthermore, the continuous variables that were highly skewed were logged to better fulfill linear regression assumptions.
Second, there is no multicollinearity in the predictors, but some of the categorical variables are redundant. Interaction effects should be tested out. There are also a lot of variables to add, which means a stepwise regression would be beneficial for variable selection.
Lastly, house sales price are clustered depending on location. The Northeast end seems to have a higher sale prices. Adding a fixed effect variable will be useful for accounting for this.

moran <- function(formula, df, response, k = 5) {
  rmse <- cv_rmse(formula, df)
  pred <- cv_pred(formula, df)
  resid_cv <- df[[response]] - pred
  
  coords <- st_coordinates(df)
  
  w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(df), k = k)), style = "W")
  
  moran_res <- moran.test(resid_cv , w_knn)
  moran_i <- moran_res$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]]
  moran_p <- moran_res$p.value
  
  tibble(
    moran_i = moran_i,
    moran_p = moran_p
  )
}

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.

Your answer:
The coefficient of age class C is -141166.45, which means that if a house is older than 60 years old, its sale price will be 141,166 dollars lower than that of a house built 20 or less years ago while holding other variables constant. The coefficient of dist_bus_mi is 40236.06, which means a 1 mile increase from a bus station will result in the house price going up by 40,000 dollars. In simple terms, the further away from a bus stop a house is, the more it will cost according to this model. Interaction terms tells us the effect of one variable on the coefficient of another. This means that when comparing the coefficient of log(house square foot) to predict sale price against the baseline community, the coefficient of log_sf in Archer Heights is 288,087 lower.
Before handing this model to an Assessor, the test CV RMSE will have to be calculated first to ensure that the model is generalizable and not massively overfitting on the train set. Due to the variable of interest being extremely skewed, the next study should log-transform sales price to create a normal distribution for linear regression. Another issue is whether the model meets the linear regression assumptions. Relationships in the real world area seldom linear and would require more complex non-linear models, which should be explored. Using more complex machine learning models should also predict sale prices more accurately.
